description:
Whether the fourth commandment remains binding depends, in Wesam Saad’s argument, on recognising different kinds of Old Testament law. He introduces moral, civil and ceremonial law, explaining their purposes and scope. Moral law is presented as universal and as revealing God’s character; civil law governed Israel’s public life; ceremonial law ordered its worship and pointed to Christ. Saad affirms that Christ fulfilled all three, while arguing that their fulfilment does not mean they all relate to Christians in the same way. The continuing Sabbath question is introduced here, with its detailed application reserved for later sessions.

The biblical case compares laws with different stated audiences, gives attention to the priority of obedience over sacrifice, and follows the distinction into Jesus’ teaching and Paul’s letters. Deuteronomy’s food provision is contrasted with the universal accountability described in Leviticus, while passages about establishing and abolishing law are read according to their context. Saad presents this as a reason to preserve moral obligation without reinstating Israel’s ceremonial requirements. He invites respectful disagreement and asks listeners to form convictions from Scripture, rather than simply borrowing a theological position. The closing discussion also stresses inward desire, not merely outward conformity, in understanding moral obedience.

questions.question: Why does the series begin with the divisions of the law?
questions.answer: Saad wants to establish how different Old Testament commands relate to Christians before deciding what remains binding in the Sabbath command. The opening session therefore supplies a framework for the later argument. It does not yet settle every question about the day or its practical observance.

questions.question: How are moral, civil and ceremonial law distinguished?
questions.answer: Moral law is described as universal obligation reflecting God’s character. Civil law regulated Israel’s social order and judicial matters. Ceremonial law concerned worship, purity and rituals that pointed to Christ’s redemptive work. These are the distinctions Saad adopts and seeks to support from Scripture.

questions.question: Does the threefold distinction mean Christ fulfilled only part of the law?
questions.answer: No. Saad expressly says that Christ fulfilled all three categories. The distinction concerns what is now binding and how fulfilment relates to each category, rather than whether Christ left some part unfulfilled. He argues for continuing moral obligation while treating Israel’s civil and ceremonial requirements differently.

questions.question: What comparison is made between Deuteronomy’s food law and Leviticus’s moral commands?
questions.answer: Saad notes that the food restriction permits an Israelite to give or sell the food to a foreigner, while the Leviticus passage holds both native and foreigner accountable for the conduct it condemns. He uses the different stated scope to support a distinction between Israel-specific ceremonial requirements and universal moral obligations.

questions.question: How is the priority of obedience over sacrifice used in the argument?
questions.answer: The prophetic passages and Jesus’ criticism of neglected weightier matters are used to show that commands are not all treated as having the same significance. Saad argues that moral obedience must not be replaced by ritual observance. He also notes that Jesus’ criticism did not tell his original hearers to neglect their other obligations.

questions.question: How does Saad relate Jesus’ teaching about worship to his teaching about the law?
questions.answer: He distinguishes the coming end of worship’s restriction to Jerusalem from the continuing moral instruction of the Sermon on the Mount. In his reading, the different contexts explain why a ceremonial arrangement can pass away while moral law is not abolished. He presents this as contextual interpretation rather than a contradiction in Jesus’ teaching.

questions.question: How are Paul’s statements about establishing and abolishing law explained?
questions.answer: Saad reads the establishment of law through faith in Romans alongside the removal of dividing ordinances in Ephesians. He argues that the former concerns moral law and the latter ceremonial distinctions separating Jew and Gentile. The answer therefore depends, in his exposition, on identifying which aspect of law each context addresses.

questions.question: Why is outward conformity an insufficient account of moral obedience?
questions.answer: In the closing discussion, Saad explains that Jesus draws attention to desires of the heart as well as external actions. He treats the commandments as a summary that can be unfolded, rather than an exhaustive list of outward acts. Listeners are urged to examine the scriptural context and form their own reasoned convictions.
